content:
The image shows a soybean field with a striking pattern: most of the field has plants that are brown/tan and fully desiccated (dead/dying), while a strip/row running through the center foreground shows green, healthy-looking plants. The surrounding plants have premature senescence — leaves have dropped, stems are brown and dry, pods are tan/dried.

Key observations:
- Whole-plant symptom (field-scale view, not leaf-level)
- Premature death/senescence across most of the field
- Green islands/strips remain (likely resistant or unaffected plants, or the disease follows a pattern suggesting soil-borne pathogen)
- No obvious foliar lesion detail visible at this scale
- The pattern of premature brown death across rows is characteristic of a root/stem rot or soil-borne pathogen

The pattern of premature plant death across a field with some surviving green plants in strips is highly characteristic of **Sudden Death Syndrome (SDS)** or **Brown Stem Rot**. SDS causes interveinal chlorosis/necrosis followed by premature defoliation, leaving brown stems standing. The field-scale pattern with abrupt transition zones fits SDS well. Brown Stem Rot also causes early senescence but tends to be more uniform. The distinct strip of green healthy plants amid a sea of dead/desiccated plants is a classic SDS field presentation, where infected plants die prematurely while escaping plants remain green.
